title: Bombay High Court bars AI misuse of Samantha Ruth Prabhu's name, image, voice
excerpt: Justice Madhav Jamdar granted ad-interim relief on October 1, restraining unauthorised use of the actress's identity across 18 defendants — including Meta, Google and Amazon — and ordering takedowns of AI deepfakes and morphed content.
body:
• The Bombay High Court on October 1, 2026 granted ad-interim relief restraining the unauthorised use of actress Samantha Ruth Prabhu's name, image and voice, including AI-generated deepfakes and morphed content.
  • Justice Madhav Jamdar held that her personality and publicity rights are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution, and her moral rights as a performer under Section 38B of the Copyright Act, 1957.
  • The suit names 18 defendants — Meta, Google, Amazon, AI platforms, digital media outlets and unidentified "John Doe" parties — with MeitY and the Department of Telecommunications added to enforce directions. Next hearing: December 10.
  • The order extends India's personality-rights line, following the Amitabh Bachchan (2022) and Anil Kapoor (2023) orders that also covered AI misuse and deepfakes.

The order

The Bombay High Court has granted actress Samantha Ruth Prabhu interim protection against the unauthorised use of her name, image and voice online. Justice Madhav Jamdar passed the ad-interim order on Thursday, October 1, 2026, in Samantha Ruth Prabhu v. John Doe & Ors., restraining the publication of content involving her identity — including deepfakes and morphed material created through artificial intelligence — and ordering the flagged content taken down.

https://x.com/DubaiNewsNow/status/2105961927960641545

Her advocate, Rashmin Khandekar, told the court her identity was being misused across websites, social media platforms and pornographic portals: photographs morphed into obscene videos and images, AI-generated voice clips, and interactive AI chatbots built to objectify her, according to Bar & Bench.

The suit names 18 defendants, including Meta Platforms (Facebook, Instagram), Google (YouTube) and Amazon, several AI platforms and digital media outlets, plus unidentified "John Doe / Ashok Kumar" parties. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) are also parties, so the court's directions can be enforced.

"The plaintiff's personality rights and publicity rights are protected by Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India, that is, the right to freedom of speech and expression, as also by Article 21 of the Constitution of India, that is, the right to life and personal liberty, including the right to privacy and the right to human dignity, and her moral rights as a performer are separately protected under Section 38B of the Copyright Act."

— Justice Madhav Jamdar, Bombay High Court

Personality rights in India: the legal backdrop

Indian courts have been steadily building personality-rights law. In November 2022, the Delhi High Court restrained the unauthorised use of Amitabh Bachchan's name, image and voice and ordered the blocking of websites running fraudulent lottery scams. In September 2023, the Delhi High Court protected Anil Kapoor against unauthorised use of his name, image, voice and likeness — including through AI, deepfakes and face morphing — In May 2024, Jackie Shroff won protection against unauthorised commercial use of his identity, including through AI, followed by orders for Arijit Singh (AI voice cloning, 2024) and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, Abhishek Bachchan and Nagarjuna (2025).

What sets Samantha's order apart is its breadth: eighteen defendants at the interim stage itself, spanning the largest global platforms and the government's enforcement arms. The court also noted intermediaries' due-diligence duties under Rule 3 of the IT Rules, 2021.

What this means for creators, fans and AI platforms

For creators, the order is a hold, not a final verdict on the technology — it restrains circulation of content built from one person's likeness and voice. But it puts synthetic-media creators on notice: chatbots, voice clones or promotional material built around a celebrity's identity without consent now carry a direct and growing legal risk in India.

For fans, reposting morphed or AI-generated content of the actress feeds the circulation the court has ordered taken down. For AI platforms, the message is that Indian courts will not wait for a dedicated deepfake statute to act.

Diaspora angle

Deepfake misuse does not respect borders, and Indian-origin performers abroad face the same exploitation on the platforms the diaspora uses daily. Because the order ropes in the global operators of Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and Amazon, its takedown directions reach the services diaspora audiences rely on — a reminder for overseas fans that resharing AI-generated celebrity content can draw enforcement action wherever it lands.

What's next

The suit is listed for further hearing on December 10, 2026. Samantha has sought permanent injunctions, damages and a John Doe order, the mechanism that lets the case proceed against unidentified infringers. She was granted leave under Clause XII of the Letters Patent on August 28, since her business and goodwill are rooted in Mumbai while several alleged infringers operate elsewhere.

The actress is currently on a maternity break and is expected to return to work next year, according to Telugu360. This case — one of the widest personality-rights orders yet passed by an Indian court — will be among the defining off-screen fights of her career.
